# LITs with `tags` `learning-theory`

*Topics — What a work is about. Nucleation holds what the Anthology of the SOTA does not: reading whose subject no anthology topic can hold. The words are seeded from the clusters the reading-time triage of 2026-09-25 found, and grow by decision.*

**Learning theory** — why learning generalizes and how it proceeds — compression and description length, Kolmogorov complexity and sufficient statistics, rate–distortion and PAC-style bounds, model selection; and training dynamics: solvable models of learning trajectories, stages, plateaus and phase transitions in training, and the implicit bias of optimisation. A work whose subject is how to train a model better is ML practice and goes to the anthology (ADR-036).

Suppose an analyst reports statistic φ_T, chosen by any data-dependent rule T from m candidates each σ-sub-Gaussian. Then the selection bias obeys \|E[φ_T − µ_T]\| ≤ σ√(2·I(T;φ)) (Prop. 1), where "information usage" I(T;φ) ≤ H(T) ≤ log m. For argmax selection over φ ~ N(µ,I) the squared error is Θ(1 + H(T)) (Prop. 3). Adaptive analyses compose additively, with I(T_{k+1};φ) ≤ Σ_i I(Y_{T_i};φ_{T_i} \| H_{i−1},T_i) (Lemma 1). Answering each query with Gaussian noise of variance σ²√j/n therefore keeps the k-th answer's error at O(σk^{1/4}/√n) (Prop. 7). | Active — read in full 2026-09-29 ([NOTE-308](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-308.md)); Worth reading as the origin of the mutual-information bias and generalisation bound that [LIT-347](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-347.md) (Xu & Raginsky) extends, and as the first place its adaptive-composition chain rule and its per-query "information budget" with Gaussian noise (½·log(1+SNR) per query) appear. Read it knowing that it is stated for a finite set of m candidate statistics, and that "the bound is tight" is shown only for Gaussian argmax and threshold selections, as squared-error (not bias) bounds except in the exponential case. |
| [LIT-369](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-369.md) v2 | Grokking and Generalization Collapse: Insights from HTSR theory | Prakash & Martin (2025), arXiv:2506.04434. A depth-3, width-200 ReLU MLP trained on 1,000 MNIST images (the Omnigrok recipe, with weights and biases scaled ×8, MSE loss, AdamW, WD = 0) for 10⁷ steps goes through three phases read off the accuracy curves. In pre-grokking (to ~10⁵ steps) training accuracy saturates while test accuracy stays low. In grokking (~10⁵–10⁶) test accuracy rises to ~0.85. In "anti-grokking" (~10⁶–10⁷) it falls to ~0.45–0.5 while training accuracy stays near 1. The average HTSR power-law exponent α of the two hidden weight matrices goes 4.0 → 2.9 → 1.1 at the phase ends (Table 1). In the collapse phase, correlation traps (outlier eigenvalues of the elementwise-shuffled weight matrix) appear. That undercuts its headline claim that α < 2 "invariably" heralds collapse. | Proposed — read in full 2026-09-30 ([NOTE-317](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-317.md)); worth knowing as the report of a late generalisation collapse after grokking at WD = 0, but it is one architecture on one 1k-sample MNIST subset, with the seed count unstated, and its central diagnostic (α < 2 ⇒ collapse) is contradicted by its own WD = 0.01 control. What would settle it: several seeds and architectures, with α and traps reported for runs that reach α < 2 without collapsing, and a comparison against the ℓ² norm under the Omnigrok LU account, which the paper does not cite. |
| [LIT-370](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-370.md) v2 | New Evidence of the Two-Phase Learning Dynamics of Neural Networks | Zhou et al. (2025), arXiv:2505.13900. VGG-16 and ResNet-20 on CIFAR-10 (SGD with momentum, lr 0.1, 160 epochs) are compared across pairs of training times. Before an early "inflection point" (~2,500 iterations for VGG-16, ~100–500 for ResNet-20), a tiny parameter perturbation under identical SGD noise sends the run to a different basin by the end: loss barrier up to ~2, test disagreement ~0.15–0.5. After it, the same perturbation leaves the runs linearly connected. Also after it, the empirical NTK keeps changing step to step but stays within a bounded cosine distance of any later reference kernel (the "cone effect", e.g. S ≈ 0.05–0.1 for VGG-16 vs ≈ 0.15–0.2 from initialisation). Switching to linearised training later gives better test accuracy (VGG-16 0.13 → 0.82 as the switch moves from ≤200 to 5,000 iterations). | Proposed — read in full 2026-09-30 ([NOTE-318](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-318.md)); a compact, readable demonstration that an early, short chaotic phase gives way to a confined, stable one in both basin and kernel terms, but it rests on two architectures on one dataset, one run each with no error bars. What would settle it: seeds and error bars, the batch size, a stated perturbation norm, other domains, and a quantitative test of confinement (e.g. an angular radius that stops growing) rather than a 3-D picture. |

Plateau end grows with population as 0.43·N^0.81 (R² = 0.998, N = 4k–256k, 5 seeds). Attention patching from post-plateau checkpoints removes the plateau, and attention from the recall position to name tokens rises through it, so the plateau is when the attention extraction circuit forms. | [LIT-373](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-373.md) v4 | The two dragons of cognition: recursive condensation for predictive processing | Li (2026), DOI-10.3389/fncom.2026.1778902. A "Hypothesis and Theory" essay proposing that the neocortex is a "biological Savitch machine". Alternating expansion ("odd parity") and contraction ("even parity") phases manufacture the disjoint closed sets of Urysohn's Lemma, and storing ("memoizing") the condensed tokens converts exponential search into polynomial "navigation". Its one non-standard formal result, Theorem 2, R(N) ∝ b^{αN} (§5.2.2, p. 11), is stated without proof. There is no data, simulation or model. The two mathematical pillars are misdescribed: Savitch's theorem saves space at the cost of time and does not memoize, and Urysohn's Lemma gives a continuous separator, not a linear one, and is not an "if and only if". | Rejected — re-read jointly with [LIT-374](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-374.md) and arXiv 2602.07974 on 2026-10-01 ([NOTE-321](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-321.md)); Read jointly with [LIT-374](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-374.md) and the companion StrLT preprint (arXiv 2602.07974), the essay is the cognitive motivation of a coherent programme: structure is discovered by costly search, condensed into frozen tokens, and reused cheaply. It is not just a misuse of two theorems. Read charitably, its mathematical slips are repairable and are not the reason to set it aside: the Urysohn "iff" and linear readout, Savitch as memoisation, the Definition 2 clash. The reason is what is left after repair: an amortised-inference and complementary-learning-systems picture already in the literature it cites; a neural mapping whose predictions do not discriminate it from standard consolidation accounts; one original quantitative claim, Theorem 2, that is not argued. A reader who wants the programme should read [LIT-374](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-374.md) and the companion, where it is made precise. |
| [LIT-374](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-374.md) v3 | Structural Decoupling: A Scaffold-Flow Theory of Generalization and Alignment | Li (2026), arXiv:2506.20699. 'Proposes "width", the least number of cells in an open cover on each of which some predictor is γ-contractive with conditional risk ≤ δ, as a structural complexity separate from VC dimension. From an additive Rademacher bound, √(2d_str log(e(K−1)n/d_str)/n) + LK·R_n(G) (Thm 4.5), it argues that context routing (the "scaffold") should be trained by different signals from within-context prediction (the "flow"), and that alignment failures are scaffold failures. The routine results are proved: coupon-collector Ω(w log w), Lipschitz composition, penalised model selection, multiclass Sauer–Shelah. The new ones are not. The phase transition at width is assumed in its proof. The bouquet witness of width/VC separation contradicts its own construction. The "fundamental theorem" is false as stated, because infinite pseudo-dimension does not prevent learnability. No theorem links the CS-Laplacian estimator to width. There are no experiments.' | Proposed — re-read jointly with [LIT-373](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-373.md) and arXiv 2602.07974 on 2026-10-01 ([NOTE-322](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-322.md)); promising and unproven. Read jointly with the companion arXiv 2602.07974, which carries the fuller statements and several definitions this paper leaves implicit. The formal core holds in repaired form: width as a structural complexity incomparable with the per-cell VC dimension; an error floor below width; the Ω(w log w) discovery cost; an additive Rademacher bound for routed predictors. The flagged slips are repairable and not load-bearing: the bouquet cover, the non-degeneracy assumption in the appendix, Massart, and pseudo-dimension against fat-shattering in Thm 4.6. What remains unproven are the claims that would make it matter: that the CS estimator converges to width itself and not to a predictor-relative count; that a monolithic model cannot match K ≥ w routing; above all, that router/scaffold training should be decoupled from task loss. This is presented as derived from the additive bound, but the bound holds for joint training too. The alignment section is asserted. What would settle it: on synthetic benchmarks of known width, (i) a K-sweep showing the floor at K < w for routed learners and its absence or presence for capacity-matched monolithic models; (ii) CS width recovery from a cold start; (iii) decoupled against joint router training, compared on forgetting and boundary error. |
| [LIT-375](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-375.md) v2 | Structural Learning Theory: A Metric-Topology Factorization Approach | Li (2026), arXiv:2602.07974. >- The formal core of Xin Li's structural-learning programme. Width w(P; γ, δ) is the least number of open cells on each of which some predictor is γ-contractive with conditional risk ≤ δ. The paper proves that width is incomparable with the per-cell VC dimension (Thm 2.2). It shows that with K < w cells there is an n-independent error floor η(w, K), under a non-degeneracy assumption stated in the body (Thm 2.4, Assumption 2.3). Width is at least c·β₁·L/D₀ under a bounded-overlap assumption (Thm 2.5), and discovering all basins costs Ω(w log w) samples (Thm 2.6). The CS-Laplacian eigenvalue count converges uniformly to the predictor-relative count w_G(P) when n ≳ (H_G + d_X log(1/r_x) + log(1/δ′))/(r_x^{d_X} g_eff²) (Thm 3.5); no result shows that w_G equals width. There are no experiments. | Proposed — read in full 2026-10-01 ([NOTE-324](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-324.md)); >- Promising and unproven. It is the programme's fullest and most careful formal statement, and it carries the learning theory of [LIT-374](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-374.md) §3 with the assumptions in the body. Its routine results hold, and its bouquet slip is repairable. What would settle it: - a theorem that the CS count for a learned predictor equals w(P; γ, δ), not w_G(P); - a K-sweep on benchmarks of known width, showing the floor at K < w for routed learners, and testing whether a capacity-matched monolithic model shows it; - the decoupled-versus-joint training comparison it motivates but does not run. |
| [LIT-376](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-376.md) v2 | Local Urysohn Width: A Topological Complexity Measure for Classification | Li (2026), arXiv:2603.15412. >- It defines local Urysohn width uw_{D₀}(P, γ): the least number of connected sets of diameter ≤ D₀, each carrying a continuous classifier correct on the margin-γ safe region it meets, needed to cover that safe region. It proves: - uw = w on a bouquet of w circles with safe balls at the antipodes, when 3γ/2 ≤ D₀ < L/2 − 3γ/4 (Thm 4.1); - uw ≥ w·m, with m = Θ(L/D₀) safe balls per loop, so uw = Ω(w·L/D₀) (Cor 5.1); - two-way non-determination with VC dimension (Thm 6.1); - an Ω(w log w) sample lower bound via label-permuted coupon collection (Thm 7.1); - uw ≥ 2β₁/Δ₀ for good, convex, bounded-adjacency covers (Thm 8.5). The proofs are correct. The obstruction is metric, as the paper concedes in Remark 8.11: patches cannot reach across the wedge point. Because Urysohn's lemma makes local correctness automatic on any patch, the measure is a connected covering number of the safe region that does not depend on the labels. | Proposed — read in full 2026-10-01 ([NOTE-323](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-323.md)); >- Promising and unproven. It is the cleanest and most honest paper in Li's programme: definitions are precise, the main theorems are correctly proved, a dependency table separates proved from conjectural results, and earlier errors are corrected openly. It is also the consistent construction that [LIT-374](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-374.md)'s and arXiv 2602.07974's bouquet lacked. What would settle it: a result showing that this width governs error or sample cost for learners not built from local experts (for example local-learning or nearest-neighbour rates), or a proof of Conj 8.9 under conditions its motivating examples actually satisfy. Without one of these, it is a covering number with a topological headline. |
| [LIT-607](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-607.md) | Natural Gradient Works Efficiently in Learning | Amari (1998), Neural Computation 10(2):251–276. When the parameter space carries a Riemannian metric G, the steepest descent direction of a loss is the natural gradient G⁻¹∇L, not the ordinary gradient. For a statistical model the metric is the Fisher information, the only invariant one. Online natural gradient learning with step 1/t is Fisher efficient: it attains the Cramér–Rao bound asymptotically, as well as the best batch estimator. The paper computes the metric and its inverse for a simple perceptron, for the group of nonsingular matrices (blind source separation, giving the update ∇L·WᵀW) and for linear systems, proposes an adaptive learning rate with 1/t convergence, and conjectures that the natural gradient escapes the plateaus of backpropagation. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-472](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-472.md)); worth reading as the source of the natural gradient: steepest descent in a Riemannian parameter space is G⁻¹∇L (Theorem 1), the Fisher information is the metric on a statistical model, and online learning with the natural gradient and a 1/t rate is Fisher efficient (Theorem 2). Its efficiency proof needs the Fisher matrix at the optimum to be invertible, which is exactly what singular learning theory says fails for neural networks. |
| [LIT-608](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-608.md) | Deep Equals Shallow for ReLU Networks in Kernel Regimes | Bietti & Bach (2021), ICLR 2021. Dot-product kernels on the sphere are diagonal in spherical harmonics, with one eigenvalue µ_k per degree k shared by N(d, k) ~ k^(d−2) harmonics. Theorem 1 reads the asymptotic decay of µ_k off the kernel function's expansion at ±1: a non-integer exponent ν there gives µ_k ~ k^(−d−2ν+1). The arc-cosine kernels have ν = 1/2 and 3/2, and composing them preserves ν, so the NTK of a deep ReLU network decays as k^(−d) and its random-feature kernel as k^(−d−2), exactly as for two layers. Deep and shallow ReLU kernels therefore have the same RKHS, the same as the Laplace kernel's for the NTK. | Active — read 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-475](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-475.md)): main text and Appendix A in full, the proofs in Appendices B and C followed at the level of their lemmas. Worth reading as the general rule behind the NTK eigenvalue decays the record holds: for a dot-product kernel on the sphere, the decay of its spherical-harmonic eigenvalues is fixed by the kernel function's non-integer exponent at the endpoints ±1 (Theorem 1). Deep ReLU kernels keep the shallow exponent, so depth leaves the spectrum's shape unchanged: µ_k ~ C(d, L) k^(−d) for the NTK and k^(−d−2) for the random-feature kernel, with only the constant growing in L (Corollaries 2–3). |
| [LIT-612](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-612.md) | The Convergence Rate of Neural Networks for Learned Functions of Different Frequencies | Basri, Jacobs, Kasten & Kritchman (2019), NeurIPS 2019. In the linearised dynamics of a wide two-layer ReLU network, on uniform data on a sphere, the Gram matrix H∞ is a convolution, so its eigenvectors are Fourier modes or spherical harmonics. Its eigenvalues are computed in closed form per frequency. Without bias, every odd frequency k ≥ 3 has eigenvalue zero, so the network cannot represent or learn it (Theorems 2 and 4). With a zero-initialised bias all frequencies pass. The eigenvalues fall as 1/k² on S¹ and, numerically, about 1/k^(d+1) on S^d, so the time to learn frequency k grows as k² and k³ on the circle and the 2-sphere. Deep and residual networks show the same exponents. | Active — read 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-481](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-481.md)): main text in full, the supplementary derivations of the S^d eigenvalues skimmed. Worth reading for the closed-form NTK eigenvalues per frequency and the exact null space they reveal. On the circle the bias-free two-layer ReLU kernel has eigenvalue 2(k²+1)/(π²(k²−1)²) on even k ≥ 2 and exactly zero on odd k ≥ 3 (Eq. 12), so such a network cannot represent cos 3θ at all (Theorems 2 and 4). A zero-initialised bias fills the null space, with 1/(π²k²) on odd k (Eq. 13). Convergence time then grows as k² on S¹ and about k³ on S², and shallow, deep and residual networks match: fitted exponents 1.93–2.15 on S¹ and 2.74–3.13 on S² (Figs. 6–7). |
| [LIT-613](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-613.md) | Traces of Class/Cross-Class Structure Pervade Deep Learning Spectra | Papyan (2020), JMLR 21(252). Cross-entropy indexes every deepnet quantity by example, class and would-be class, a two-way MANOVA layout. In the spectra of features, backpropagated errors, gradients, the Fisher, the Hessian and weights, knockouts attribute the top outlier to the global mean, C−1 outliers to between-class second moment, a mini-bulk of C(C−1) to between-cross-class covariance, and the main bulk to within-cross-class covariance. Feature and error class means separate from the bulk and become orthogonal with depth. Gradient class means are approximately feature class means ⊗ error class means, layer by layer; K-FAC's single Kronecker product misaligns the Fisher's outliers and the class-wise CFAC aligns them. For multinomial logistic regression on a Gaussian class model the expected Fisher spectrum is derived exactly. | Active — read 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-474](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-474.md)); worth reading as the general account of class/cross-class structure in deepnet spectra: features, backpropagated errors, gradients, Fisher, Hessian and weights all show one outlier from the global mean, C−1 from class means, a mini-bulk of about C(C−1) from cross-class means, and a main bulk from within-class variation. Per layer, gradient class means are approximately Kronecker products of feature class means and error class means, which is why K-FAC, pairing every class with every class, misaligns the Fisher's outliers, and CFAC, pairing each class with itself, aligns them. Proved only for multinomial logistic regression on a Gaussian model. |
| [LIT-616](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-616.md) | A Widely Applicable Bayesian Information Criterion | Watanabe (2012), arXiv:1208.6338; JMLR 14:867–897 (2013). A model is singular when the parameter-to-distribution map is not one-to-one or the Fisher information is not positive definite: neural networks, mixtures, reduced-rank regression, HMMs. Its Bayes free energy is nL_n(w0) + λ log n − (m − 1) log log n + O_p(1), with λ the real log canonical threshold (RLCT), not d/2. WBIC, the posterior average of nL_n(w) at inverse temperature 1/log n, has the same leading terms even for singular, unrealizable models, equals BIC for regular ones, and needs no knowledge of the true distribution. Two temperatures give an estimate of λ. In reduced-rank regression WBIC picked the true rank in 100 of 100 trials and recovered theoretical RLCTs closely. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-473](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-473.md)); worth reading as the record's lawful, short statement of the core of singular learning theory, standing in for Watanabe's unread book ([LIT-354](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-354.md)). It states the Bayes free energy asymptotics F = nL_n(w0) + λ log n − (m − 1) log log n + O_p(1), with λ the real log canonical threshold and m its multiplicity (Theorem 2), and defines λ through resolution of singularities (Theorem 1, Eq. 18). Its own result is WBIC, the posterior mean of nL_n(w) at inverse temperature 1/log n, which matches F to the λ log n term even for singular and unrealizable models (Theorem 4), equals BIC for regular ones (Theorem 5), and estimates λ from two temperatures (Corollary 3). The prior results are stated with citations to the book, not re-proved. |
| [LIT-617](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-617.md) | The Full Spectrum of Deepnet Hessians at Scale: Dynamics with SGD Training and Sample Size | Papyan (2018), arXiv. Stochastic Lanczos without reorthogonalization (O(Mnp) time, O(p) memory) plus subspace-iteration deflation measures the full Hessian spectrum of VGG11 and ResNet18 on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10/100, over 16,000 trained models. It confirms a bulk with about C outliers, attributes the outliers to the Gauss–Newton term G and most of the bulk to the residual H, finds H's spectrum symmetric with a power-law tail rather than Marchenko–Pastur, and finds H never negligible. Version 2 decomposes G into class means (outliers), cross-class variation and within-class variation (two bulks) and tracks them across epochs and sample sizes. | Active — read 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-478](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-478.md)); worth reading as the measurement that the bulk-and-C-outliers spectrum of the Hessian persists at full scale (VGG11, 28M parameters), that the outliers belong to the Gauss–Newton/Fisher term G and the bulk mostly to the residual H, and, in its second version, that G splits into class means (outliers) and two bulks (cross-class and within-class variation). Its tools are stochastic Lanczos spectral density estimation without reorthogonalization, plus subspace-iteration deflation. |
| [LIT-618](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-618.md) | Prevalence of Neural Collapse during the terminal phase of deep learning training | Papyan, Han & Donoho (2020), PNAS 117(40). Training past zero error (the terminal phase, TPT) drives four linked phenomena in the last layer: within-class variability collapses (Tr(Σ_WΣ_B†)/C → 0), centred class means become equinorm and equiangular with cosines −1/(C−1), a simplex ETF; classifier rows become proportional to the means; and the decision becomes nearest class mean. Measured on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-10/100, STL10 and ImageNet with VGG, ResNet and DenseNet, 480 models. Test accuracy and DeepFool robustness keep improving during TPT. Theorems: NC1–NC2 imply NC3–NC4 for the Webb–Lowe and Soudry max-margin classifiers, and the simplex ETF uniquely maximizes the small-noise error exponent. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-476](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-476.md)); worth reading as the source of neural collapse: in the terminal phase of training, last-layer features collapse to their class means (NC1), the centred means form a simplex equiangular tight frame (NC2), the classifier aligns with them (NC3) and the decision becomes nearest class centre (NC4). Measured on 7 datasets × 3 architectures; NC1–NC2 imply NC3–NC4 for the Webb–Lowe and max-margin classifiers, and the simplex ETF is the unique optimal codebook in a vanishing-noise Gaussian channel. It explains Papyan's Hessian outliers as class means outgrowing collapsing within-class variation. |
| [LIT-619](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-619.md) | Measurements of Three-Level Hierarchical Structure in the Outliers in the Spectrum of Deepnet Hessians | Papyan (2019), ICML. For a C-class network the Gauss–Newton term of the Hessian is G = (1/n)ΔΔᵀ, a second moment (not covariance) of logit derivatives δᵢ,c,c′ indexed by example, true class and logit. Grouping them into C² group means δc,c′ and C clusters with centres δc gives G = G₀ + G₁ + G₂ + G₃ (Eq. 28). The top-C outliers of G are those of G₁ = (C−1)Ave_c δcδcᵀ, because clusters are far apart and tight. Early in training the group means cluster by logit c′, later by true class c. Holds across MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10 and ImageNet with VGG, ResNet and DenseNet; the outliers exceed their approximations slightly, as random matrix theory would predict. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-479](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-479.md)); worth reading as the paper that explains the C outliers of the deepnet Hessian: the Gauss–Newton/Fisher term G is a second moment, not a covariance, of logit derivatives indexed by (example, class, logit), and the C outliers are the eigenvalues of G₁ = (C−1)·Ave_c δ_c δ_cᵀ, the C class-cluster centres, computable from a C×C Gram matrix without high-dimensional eigenanalysis. The match is empirical, over 18,000 trained models. |
| [LIT-623](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-623.md) | Bayesian Interpolation | MacKay (1992), Neural Computation 4(3):415–447. Two levels of inference: fit each model, then rank models by their evidence P(D\|H). Under a Gaussian approximation the evidence is the best-fit likelihood times an Occam factor, the ratio of posterior to prior accessible parameter volume, so complex or finely tuned models penalise themselves (Eqs. 5–6). For linear interpolation with quadratic regularisers the evidence sets the regularising constant and the noise level through γ, the number of well-determined parameters (2αE_W = γ, 2βE_D = N − γ). It ranks polynomial, radial-basis, spline, Hermite and neural-network models on two data sets. In expectation, no fixed model's log evidence beats the true model's. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-471](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-471.md)); worth reading as the source of the evidence framework and the Occam factor in the form the field uses: evidence ≈ best-fit likelihood × Occam factor, the Occam factor being the ratio of posterior to prior accessible parameter volume, (2π)^{k/2} det^{-1/2}A · P(w_MP\|H) under a Gaussian approximation (Eqs. 5–6). It also gives the "number of good parameter measurements" γ = Σ λ_a/(λ_a + α), which sets the regularising constant (2αE_W = γ) and the noise level (2βE_D = N − γ) at the evidence maximum. The framework is Gull and Skilling's, as MacKay says, and every demonstration is one-dimensional interpolation. Flagged anthology-candidate for its regularisation and early-stopping arguments. |
| [LIT-624](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-624.md) | Towards Understanding the Spectral Bias of Deep Learning | Cao, Fang, Wu, Zhou & Gu (2019). For a two-layer ReLU network trained by gradient descent on squared loss, the training residual projected onto the eigenfunctions of the NTK integral operator with the r_k largest eigenvalues decays like (1 − λ_(r_k))^T (Theorem 4.2). This holds for any labelling, provided the sample size beats the eigengap and the width is polynomial in λ_(r_k)^(−1). On uniform data on S^d the eigenfunctions are spherical harmonics, with µ_k = Ω(k^(−d−1)) for k ≫ d and Ω(d^(−k+1)) for d ≫ k on even degrees, and µ_k = 0 on odd k ≥ 3 (Theorem 4.3). Lower degrees are learned first, faster, and with fewer samples and narrower networks. | Active — read 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-483](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-483.md)): main text and Appendix A in full, the proofs in Appendix B followed at the level of their lemmas. Worth reading as the theorem that makes "spectral bias" a statement about NTK eigendirections: for a two-layer ReLU network trained by gradient descent, the residual projected onto the top r_k eigenfunctions of the NTK integral operator shrinks like (1 − λ_(r_k))^T (Theorem 4.2), for any target, with sample size governed by the eigengap λ_(r_k) − λ_(r_k+1). On uniform spherical data the eigenfunctions are spherical harmonics, the odd degrees above 1 have eigenvalue zero, and µ_k = Ω(max(k^(−d−1), d^(−k+1))) for even k (Theorem 4.3). |

On the synthetic task the peak coincides with the best OOD early-exit accuracy while ID accuracy keeps rising. On a synthetic arithmetic task with GPT-2 Small the peak (0.27 at layer 10 of 12) is where OOD early-exit accuracy is best (56.9%) while ID accuracy keeps rising to 93.2% at layer 12. Learned residual scales put less weight on the final layers when fitted on OOD data. | [LIT-663](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-663.md) | Taxonomizing local versus global structure in neural network loss landscapes | Yang, Hodgkinson, Theisen, Zou, Gonzalez, Ramchandran & Mahoney (2021), NeurIPS. Two transitions give four phases: I sharp and poorly connected, II sharp and well connected, III flat and poorly connected, IV flat and well connected, with IV split by CKA into IV-A and IV-B. Test accuracy is best in IV-B. Sharpness alone mispredicts accuracy across phases, and in phase III training to zero loss does worse than stopping in the sharp phases. Double descent appears as a dark band at the phase boundary under label noise. | Active — read 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-516](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-516.md)); worth reading as the empirical taxonomy of loss landscapes by local and global structure: Hessian top eigenvalue and trace separate locally sharp from locally flat, Bezier-curve mode connectivity between independently trained models separates globally poorly-connected from well-connected, and CKA similarity of their outputs splits the well-connected, flat phase in two. Across a load-like by temperature-like grid (width, data amount or label noise against batch size, learning rate or weight decay), the best test accuracy sits in the flat, well-connected, high-similarity phase IV-B; the Hessian alone mispredicts, and where connectivity is poor, training to zero loss can lower test accuracy. | [LIT-667](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-667.md) | Does Data Scaling Lead to Visual Compositional Generalization? | Uselis, Dittadi & Oh (2025), ICML 2025. Two labelled concepts with n values each form an n × n grid; training shows k combinations per value and testing uses the rest. On dSprites, 3DShapes, PUG, colored MNIST and a new FSprites, ResNet-50s trained from scratch reach near 100% on seen pairs and fall sharply on unseen ones; 4× more in-distribution data does not close the gap, while more values and more combinations do. Under exact linear factorization, k = 2 combinations per value suffice for a linear classifier to get all unseen pairs right (Proposition 4.1). DINO, DINOv2 and CLIP features are partly factored. Mode connectivity follows from generic robustness properties of trained nets. Conversely, for any width there is a dataset on which global minima of a two-layer student are disconnected, so connectivity is a property of the solutions training finds. Checked on MNIST convnets and VGG-11 on CIFAR-10. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-544](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-544.md)); the first explanation of mode connectivity that applies to realistic multilayer nets. If two solutions can each lose half their units per layer at a cost of at most ε in loss (dropout stability), they are joined by a piecewise-linear path whose loss never exceeds the worse endpoint by more than ε; a stronger noise-stability condition gives 10 segments. A counterexample shows that connectivity fails for some global minima of arbitrarily overparametrized two-layer nets, so the property belongs to the solutions training finds, not to the landscape. The conditions are checked on small MNIST convnets and one VGG-11 trained with channel-wise dropout. |

Zhang et al.'s observations, that deep networks fit noisy labels and that only early stopping regularizes them, are read through the statistical mechanics of learning. A Very Simple Deep Learning model has two control parameters: a load α = m_eff/N, lowered by randomizing labels, and a temperature τ, raised by stopping early. In the thermodynamic limit (m, N → ∞, α fixed), generalization error can drop discontinuously at a critical αc, and a two-dimensional (α, τ) phase diagram has a spin-glass-like overtraining phase. The mechanism is entropy–energy competition, shown on the continuous and Ising perceptrons: the Ising entropy vanishes near zero error, so the first-order condition loses its interior solution. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-542](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-542.md)); worth reading as the position paper that brought the statistical-mechanics theory of generalization back to deep learning: a network is idealized as a black box governed by a load-like parameter α (effective data per capacity, lowered by label noise) and a temperature-like parameter τ (raised by early stopping), and in the thermodynamic limit m, N → ∞ with α = m/N fixed, generalization has phases with sharp transitions. The mechanism is shown on the continuous versus Ising perceptron: where the entropy of near-optimal hypotheses vanishes (s(ε) ~ −(π²/2)ε² ln ε), the error drops discontinuously at αc, which PAC/VC bounds do not even qualitatively describe. A qualitative argument with no new theorem and no experiment. |

GCN solutions for node classification from different seeds are connected by quadratic Bezier curves but often separated on the straight line, more so on co-authorship and heterophilous graphs than on citation graphs. GNN variants (GCN, GraphSAGE, GAT) give similar barriers, MLPs different ones. On CSBM graphs, barriers fall with density and feature separability and are highest at middling homophily. The authors bound the barrier through the spectral gap, bound the generalisation gap by the barrier, and propose a Wasserstein distance between graphs' interpolation-loss curves that correlates with transfer gaps. | Proposed — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-529](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-529.md)); watching, as the first study of mode connectivity in graph neural networks. Two GCNs trained on the same graph with different seeds are usually joined by a low-loss quadratic Bezier curve but often not by a straight line, and the barrier depends on the graph more than on the GNN variant: it falls with density, with feature separability, and with homophily far from one half, in synthetic CSBM graphs and, by the authors' reading, in 12 real ones. A loss-barrier bound, a generalisation bound in terms of the barrier, and a barrier-based distance between graphs are stated, but the appendix that should hold the proofs does not; the v1 text still carries an editor's placeholder. What would settle it: the proofs, and numbers for the barriers the figures show. |
| [LIT-678](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-678.md) | Intermediate Layer Classifiers for OOD generalization | Uselis & Oh (2025), ICLR 2025. Linear probes on the frozen features of an intermediate layer (ILCs) are compared with last-layer retraining for out-of-distribution classification on CMNIST, Waterbirds, CelebA, MultiCelebA, CIFAR-10C, CIFAR-100C and ImageNet variants, with ResNets and ViTs. | [LIT-679](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-679.md) | A Random Matrix Analysis of Random Fourier Features: Beyond the Gaussian Kernel, a Precise Phase Transition, and the Corresponding Double Descent | Liao, Couillet & Mahoney (2020), NeurIPS 2020 and J. Stat. Mech. (2021). For random Fourier features ΣX = [cos(WX); sin(WX)] with n, p, N large and comparable, the expected resolvent of ΣXᵀΣX/n is asymptotically Q̄ = ((N/n)(Kcos/(1+δcos) + Ksin/(1+δsin)) + λI)⁻¹, with δσ = (1/n)tr KσQ̄, not the Gaussian-kernel prediction. Closed forms for training and test MSE follow and match MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and Kannada-MNIST. In the ridgeless limit the δ jump at 2N = n, separating an under- and an over-parameterized phase; the test MSE diverges there unless test data sit within about λ of the training data, which is the double-descent peak. A tuned λ removes it. | Active — read 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-519](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-519.md)); worth reading as an exact random-matrix account of double descent in random Fourier feature ridge regression when n, p and N are large together: the RFF Gram matrix does not converge to the Gaussian kernel in spectral norm, but its resolvent has a deterministic equivalent built from the cos and sin kernels with corrections δcos, δsin solving a fixed point (Theorem 1). Training and test MSE follow in closed form (Theorems 2–3). As λ → 0 the δ jump from O(1) to order 1/λ across 2N = n, so the model has two phases, and the test error diverges at the boundary when test data differ from training data; that singularity is the double-descent peak. Data need only be concentrated random vectors, not Gaussian. |
| [LIT-683](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-683.md) | Exact expressions for double descent and implicit regularization via surrogate random design | Dereziński, Liang & Mahoney (2019), NeurIPS 2020. For the Moore–Penrose estimator X⁺y in linear regression, a determinantal surrogate design (density ∝ pdet(XXᵀ), Poisson sample size with mean n) gives exact MSE: σ² tr((Σ + λnI)⁻¹)(1 − αn)/(d − n) + w*ᵀ(Σ + λnI)⁻¹w*·(d − n)/tr((Σ + λnI)⁻¹) for n < d, σ² tr(Σ⁻¹) at n = d, σ² tr(Σ⁻¹)(1 − βn)/(n − d) for n > d, where n = tr(Σ(Σ + λnI)⁻¹). The surrogate agrees with the i.i.d. design as d, n → ∞ for sub-Gaussian data. | Active — read 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-518](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-518.md)); worth reading as the exact, non-asymptotic account of double descent and implicit regularization for minimum-norm least squares: replacing the i.i.d. design by a determinantal "surrogate" design gives closed-form MSE in every regime (Theorem 1) and shows that, below the interpolation threshold n < d, the expected minimum-norm solution equals the population ridge solution with the λn for which the ridge effective dimension tr(Σ(Σ + λnI)⁻¹) equals n (Theorem 2). The surrogate matches the i.i.d. design asymptotically for sub-Gaussian data (Theorem 3), at an empirically O(1/d) rate. | [LIT-792](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-792.md) | Transformers learn in-context by gradient descent | von Oswald, Niklasson, Randazzo, Sacramento, Mordvintsev, Zhmoginov and Vladymyrov (2022), ICML 2023. Proposition 1 constructs weights for which one linear self-attention layer transforms each token (x_j, y_j) to (x_j, y_j − ΔW x_j), with ΔW one gradient step on the context's squared loss, so the query token's read-out equals the prediction of the updated linear model. | [LIT-796](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-796.md) | The Surprising Effectiveness of Test-Time Training for Few-Shot Learning | Akyürek, Damani, Zweiger, Qiu, Guo, Pari, Kim and Andreas (2024), ICML 2025. Test-time training here is a temporary, per-task LoRA update of a language model on a loss built from the task's own demonstrations, discarded afterwards. | [LIT-797](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-797.md) | An Explanation of In-context Learning as Implicit Bayesian Inference | Xie, Raghunathan, Liang and Ma (2021), ICLR 2022. Models pretraining text as a mixture of HMMs indexed by a latent concept θ and assumes the LM fits it exactly; in-context prediction is then the posterior predictive, and Theorem 1 shows the in-context predictor reaches the Bayes-optimal 0-1 risk as the number of examples grows, when each example's KL signal about θ exceeds the error from the low-probability transitions between examples. | [LIT-801](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-801.md) | Learning to (Learn at Test Time): RNNs with Expressive Hidden States | Sun, Li, Dalal, Xu, Vikram, Zhang, Dubois, Chen, Wang, Koyejo, Hashimoto and Guestrin (2024), ICML 2025. Makes a sequence layer's hidden state the weights W of an inner model f, updated per token by a gradient step on a learned self-supervised reconstruction loss, with output f(θ_Q x_t; W_t). Two exact identities follow: a linear inner model with batch gradient descent is linear attention (Theorem 1), and the Nadaraya–Watson estimator as inner learner is softmax self-attention (Theorem 2). The empirical part, TTT-Linear and TTT-MLP against Mamba and a Transformer at 125M–1.3B, is an architecture result that belongs to the anthology's question. |
| [LIT-855](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-855.md) | Closed-Form Training Dynamics Reveal Learned Features and Linear Structure in Word2Vec-like Models | Karkada, Simon, Bahri and DeWeese (2025), [ARXIV-2502.09863](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.09863), NeurIPS 2025. The quartic approximation of word2vec's loss, under symmetric reweighting with constant aggregate weight, is exactly unweighted factorisation of M*, the co-occurrence matrix's relative deviation from independence, and from small initialisation gradient flow learns M*'s eigenvectors one at a time in sigmoidal steps. The embeddings this predicts match word2vec's features and benchmark scores far better than truncated PMI or PPMI factorisations do. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-660](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-660.md)); worth reading as the first closed-form account of what a contrastive word-embedding algorithm learns under a rank constraint, and in what order. Replacing word2vec's logistic loss by its quartic Taylor approximation, and choosing symmetric reweightings whose aggregate weight is constant, turns the objective into unweighted symmetric matrix factorisation of M*, the matrix of relative deviations of word co-occurrence from independence (Theorem 1, proved). From vanishing random initialisation, gradient flow then learns the eigenvectors of M* one at a time, each by a sigmoidal step in time (ln(λ_k/σ²))/λ_k (Result 3, a derivation that drops terms, not a proof). | [LIT-857](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-857.md) | Single-Head Attention in High Dimensions: A Theory of Generalization, Weights Spectra, and Scaling Laws | Boncoraglio, Erba, Troiani, Xu, Krzakala and Zdeborová (2025), arXiv. Weight decay on the factor is exactly a nuclear-norm penalty on the product. | [LIT-858](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-858.md) | Towards Understanding Grokking: An Effective Theory of Representation Learning | Liu, Kitouni, Nolte, Michaud, Tegmark and Williams (2022), NeurIPS 2022. In a toy model that decodes the sum of two learned embeddings, grokking is representation learning: an unseen pair is answered correctly when its embedding sum equals a trained pair's, and the critical training fraction (about 0.4 for addition with p = 10) is where the training set's "parallelogram" equations first fix the embedding up to translation and scale. A posited effective loss on the normalised embeddings predicts that threshold and, through its third Hessian eigenvalue, the time to structure. An unseen pair is predicted correctly when its embedding sum coincides with a trained pair's (a "parallelogram"), and the critical training fraction is where the training set's parallelogram equations first fix the embedding up to translation and scale. The account is exact for the toy (1D embeddings, addition hard-coded in the architecture, an effective loss posited and derived only for a linear decoder); the transformer and MNIST evidence is qualitative (PCA pictures and phase diagrams), and the four "phases" are defined by accuracy thresholds, not by any order parameter. |
| [LIT-859](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-859.md) | Exact Learning Dynamics of In-Context Learning in Linear Transformers and Its Application to Non-Linear Transformers | Mainali and Teixeira (2025), [ARXIV-2504.12916](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.12916). For a single linear attention layer trained by small-step SGD on in-context regression ℝᵈ → ℝᵈ, with the input covariance and every task matrix sharing one eigenbasis and the weights assumed to stay in it, the averaged dynamics decouple into one logistic equation per eigenmode: mode α is learned on a timescale τ_α = (ηP s_α²)⁻¹, giving plateaus and cliffs in the loss, and settles where p_α q_α = N / ((N+1)s_α + Tr S), so the trained predictor applies an inverse, finite-N-corrected training covariance to the context's empirical covariance. | [LIT-862](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-862.md) | A mathematical theory of semantic development in deep neural networks | Saxe, McClelland and Ganguli (2019), PNAS 116(23):11537–11546, [ARXIV-1810.10531](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.10531). A two-layer linear network trained from small weights learns the singular modes of its input–output correlations one at a time, each in a sigmoidal step at a time of order (τ/s)ln(s/ε), where a shallow network learns them all at once. With data generated on a tree this gives coarse-to-fine differentiation in stages, transient illusory correlations and narrowing generalisation; the SVD also defines typicality, prototypes and category coherence, and minimum-norm weights fix the hidden similarity matrix across networks. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-666](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-666.md)); worth reading as the paper that turns the exactly solved learning dynamics of a two-layer linear network into a theory of semantic development. Trained by gradient descent from small weights on whitened inputs, the network learns the singular modes of the item–feature correlation matrix one at a time, each by a sigmoid at a time of order (τ/s)ln(s/ε), while a shallow network learns every mode on one exponential timescale. Hierarchically generated data have singular values that fall with depth in the tree, so broad distinctions are learned first in stage-like transitions, individual predictions can rise and fall between stages, and inductive generalisation narrows with development. The same SVD gives typicality, prototypes and a coherence threshold (a BBP transition), rings give Fourier modes, and minimum-norm weights, which small initialisation approximates, give identical hidden similarity matrices across networks. | [LIT-864](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-864.md) | Exact solutions to the nonlinear dynamics of learning in deep linear neural networks | Saxe, McClelland and Ganguli (2014), [ARXIV-1312.6120](https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.6120), ICLR 2014. Solves gradient-descent learning in deep linear networks with whitened inputs from decoupled initial weights: each singular mode of the input–output correlation is learned by a sigmoid at a time of order (τ/s)ln(s/ε), with conserved differences of squared layer strengths. For any depth, the delay depth adds is set by the initial end-to-end mode strength, finite as depth grows when that strength is of order one and the step size is scaled with depth. Argues, with simulations, that scaled Gaussian layers are not isometric in product while orthogonal ones are, and that tanh networks with orthogonal weights near gain 1 stay close to isometric. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-667](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-667.md)); worth reading as the paper in which the learning dynamics of deep linear networks were solved exactly from decoupled starts at any depth (Fukumizu had solved one hidden layer for another class of starts) and the stepwise, mode-by-mode picture was set out that later work calls Saxe-style. Gradient descent on a linear network with one hidden layer and whitened inputs is a cubic system whose modes cooperate within a singular mode of the input–output correlations and repel across modes; from decoupled initial weights each mode's strength follows a sigmoid reaching s at a time of about (τ/s)ln(s/ε), with a conserved difference of squared layer strengths and, in the appendix, the unbalanced case. Beyond what the 2019 restatement keeps, it solves arbitrary depth from decoupled starts: depth slows learning through the initial end-to-end mode strength, so from strength of order one the number of iterations stays finite as depth grows once the step size is scaled down with depth, while from strength ε the delay grows like s/ε. It argues that scaled Gaussian layers preserve norms but not isometry, that random orthogonal layers give depth-independent learning times on MNIST, and that tanh networks with orthogonal weights near gain 1 keep the end-to-end Jacobian's singular values of order one. Random initial weights, the role of isometry in learning time and everything nonlinear rest on simulation, not proof. |
| [LIT-877](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-877.md) | How Deep Neural Networks Learn Compositional Data: The Random Hierarchy Model | Cagnetta, Petrini, Tomasini, Favero and Wyart (2023; Phys. Rev. X 14, 031001, 2024). Introduces the Random Hierarchy Model, a random context-free grammar of depth L with m synonymic expansions per symbol. Shallow and lazy networks need a fixed fraction of all data, exponential in the input dimension; deep feature-learning CNNs learn from about n_c m^L examples, polynomial in it, which is where hidden layers become invariant to swapping synonyms and where the class statistics of input patches, equal for synonyms, emerge from sampling noise. Without those correlations deep networks fail too. The law is measured; the link to correlations is a scaling argument plus a one-step-gradient model. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-677](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-677.md)); worth reading as the paper that introduces the Random Hierarchy Model, a random context-free grammar of fixed depth L and branching s in which each class and each higher-level feature has m interchangeable ("synonymic") lower-level representations, and as a measured and partly derived account of how many examples a deep network needs to learn it. Two-layer networks and lazy (kernel-regime) deep networks need a fixed fraction of all the data, which is exponential in the input dimension d = s^L; deep convolutional networks in a feature-learning parametrisation need P* ≈ n_c m^L, a power of d. That number is measured, not proved. It coincides with the training-set size at which the networks' hidden layers become insensitive to swapping synonyms, and with the size at which the class-conditional frequencies of input s-tuples, which are equal for synonyms, rise above sampling noise; a one-step gradient argument for a two-layer network on one patch links the last two. Removing the input–label correlations, with the hierarchy kept, makes deep networks fail again. The hierarchy is one of constituency (parts composing wholes), not of attributes implying attributes. |
